item.title: Anthropic chief says claims that he wants humans to ‘surrender’ to AI are ‘absurd’
item.description: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei on Wednesday denied wanting humanity to give up its free will to AI, calling it “absurd” to attribute the idea to him as rival tech leaders push back.
item.dc:creator: AFP Staff
item.content:encoded: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei on Wednesday denied wanting humanity to give up its free will to AI, calling it “absurd” to attribute the idea to him as rival tech leaders push back. “No, I do not believe that we should ‘surrender human free will’ to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do,” Amodei wrote in a lengthy post on X, a week after Anthropic’s record-setting stock market debut. “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he added. Fears that AI tools could slip out of human control have haunted Silicon Valley since a string of incidents this summer, including the hacking of Hugging Face by autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” an Anthropic safety lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote in September. Amodei took aim, without naming names, at “some AI CEOs” who repeat slogans like “AI should be just a tool” but then are not “actually doing anything different in their products.” On Sunday, Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang wrote on X that “we should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said earlier this month that if the tradeoff for curing cancer is “you are going to lose all agency and control and voice in the future,” that is “a terrible sales pitch.” Amodei’s post was in response to an article by US outlet Axios on AI debate, though he did not address his previous remarks on the topic. In February, Amodei told The New York Times that in “life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over” to AI. And in late 2024, he predicted that AI systems “will be the leaders, and they’ll be ordering humans or other AI systems around.” On Wednesday, he acknowledged that “we may want limits” on recursive self-improvement, or RSI, in which AI models can autonomously create new versions of itself, and that “we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously,” without saying where the line should be drawn. Yet in its IPO filing, Anthropic said that “each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next,” and that Claude wrote over 90 percent of the contributions to its codebase in September. Elon Musk, who has long predicted that superintelligent AI would leave humans “like pet Labradors,” reposted Amodei’s statement with a one-word comment: “interesting.”

item.title: Global stocks rise and tech shares rebound as U.S. closes for Thanksgiving
item.description: U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: HONG KONG — Shares advanced in Europe and Asia on Thursday while U.S. markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday. Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence helped push benchmarks in Asia higher, though some profit-taking by investors toward the end of the day pared those gains. Investors have been growing cautious about the AI trade. They also are watching for impacts from the latest tariff hikes Washington plans to impose on China, Japan, the European Union and other trading partners. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX jumped 1.9 per cent to 25,180.12, while France’s CAC 40 climbed 1.8 per cent to 8,126.47. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 1.6 per cent to 10,591.83. U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rebounded and closed 0.9 per cent higher at 57,499.16. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 7.3 per cent, while memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings surged 12.6 per cent. Shares of chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron were up 0.6 per cent. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index added 0.3 per cent to 4,711.21 after a 6.2 per cent drop a day earlier. Samsung Electronics gained 0.4 per cent, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix rose 2.2 per cent. Taiwan’s Taiex was 2.5 per cent higher. But shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., edged 0.2 per cent lower. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index was 1.2 per cent higher at 22,226.88. The Shanghai Composite index was up less than 0.1 per cent at 3,476.88. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.8 per cent to 8,763.80. India’s Sensex rose 0.5 per cent. Wall Street closed mixed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The benchmark S&P 500 index lost 0.3 per cent Wednesday after falling as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed 0.6 per cent lower, after recovering from a drop of as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average picked up 0.3 per cent. Nvidia fell 3.9 per cent as AI shares lost steam for a second day after Jensen Huang’s comeback as CEO. On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings warned it could downgrade Nvidia’s credit rating over concerns surrounding its management and governance. Broadcom, which had fallen sharply earlier in the day, was 0.1 per cent lower at the close. Anthropic, which began public trading last week, recovered from an early drop and ended 1.1 per cent higher, though still below its IPO, or initial public offering, price of US$83 per share. In commodities trading, oil prices climbed early Thursday as tensions in the Middle East persisted even as global oil supply continued to recover. Brent crude, the international standard, was 0.5 per cent higher at $91.09 per barrel. It was trading at approximately $72 a barrel before the war began in late February. Benchmark U.S. crude gained one per cent to $84.51 per barrel. Recent reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global oil transport, have contributed to concerns over oil flows and “brought supply risks back into focus,” ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a commentary Thursday. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.30 Japanese yen from 159.16 yen. The euro was trading at $1.0968, down from $1.0974. Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

item.title: Auto sector in Canada is moving away from U.S. imports: DesRosiers
item.description: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war. The data analysis from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars. That result is down from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. Meanwhile, most other markets saw their shares rise from two years ago. The proportion of Canada’s light vehicle imports from Mexico increased from 16.7 per cent in 2024 to 20.5 per cent so far this year, while Japan saw an increase to 12.9 per cent from 10.7 per cent in 2024. Imports from South Korea have risen from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent, and the combined European markets saw a bump from 9.8 to 11.1 per cent. Aside from Canada’s southern neighbour, China was the only market behind its 2024 share at 2.6 per cent thus far in 2026, down from 2.9 per cent. The overall shift is notable given that not all manufacturers are affected by Canada’s counter-tariffs, which exclude some of the highest volume players, the report said. DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King said certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation “have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible and to continue to provide Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price.” “What the U.S. lost in share was captured readily by the other major light vehicle exporters, with the trade war helping to diversify Canada’s sourcing in this space,” he said in a statement. Vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content, while auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico agreement on trade are exempt.  In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. Canada maintains import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with CUSMA. Ottawa allows automakers to import a quota of vehicles made in the United States tariff-free, based in part on their level of automotive assembly in Canada. Automotive analyst Daniel Ross said the figures show manufacturers are “fighting ... to keep prices from climbing.” “I think it’s directly related to trade policy and the trade war at hand,” said Ross, senior manager of auto industry insights at Canadian Black Book. “A lot of manufacturers are finding their way to decrease dependency for the Canadian market based off of what’s happening in the U.S. So the narrative is, ultimately, where else can we get these? Where is it easier? Where can we work with?” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent weeks that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector. Whether automakers continue to shift imports to non-U.S. markets will depend on how trade negotiations progress, said Ross. “If it were not to move (in a positive) direction, then I think we could continue to see that climb of market share for Mexico, for Japan specifically,” he said. “Whether or not that’s the best way forward, it’s a better way forward than having our skin in the game with a U.S. marketplace that’s highly volatile for the last few years.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

item.title: When Wall Street’s fear gauges flash red, what happens next?: Stan Wong
item.description: While heightened market volatility can create considerable anxiety, history suggests that periods of extreme pessimism have frequently been followed by strong equity market returns.
item.content:encoded:
“Be fearful when others are greedy and be greedy when others are fearful.” Warren Buffett’s famous advice captures a fundamental principle of investing: some of the most attractive opportunities emerge when investor confidence is at its lowest. While heightened market volatility can create considerable anxiety, history suggests that periods of extreme pessimism have frequently been followed by strong equity market returns.

Wall Street’s fear gauges are flashing red Two measures of this anxiety are the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) and Nasdaq-100 Volatility Index (VXN) , commonly known as Wall Street’s “fear gauges.” Derived from options prices, they measure expected volatility over the next 30 days for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively. These indicators typically rise when markets decline and investors seek protection against further losses. Higher readings signal expectations for larger market fluctuations, not their direction. Historically, VIX readings below 20 generally reflect calmer conditions, while readings above 30 indicate heightened anxiety. At extreme levels, these fear gauges can also serve as contrarian indicators, suggesting that investor pessimism may have become excessive. Last Friday, Nov. 20, the VIX closed at 35.9 and the VXN at 45.3. Comparable spikes occurred following sweeping U.S. tariff announcements in April 2025, during the inflation-driven bear market of 2022 and amid the COVID-19 market collapse in March 2020. Each period demonstrated how quickly investor confidence can deteriorate. But what does history tell us about what happens after fear reaches such extreme levels? What 25 years of market history reveal My analysis of Bloomberg data over the past 25 years examined subsequent 12-month equity returns following elevated volatility readings, using non-overlapping observation windows to avoid counting repeated signals during the same periods of turbulence. For the S&P 500, nine completed qualifying signals occurred when the VIX rose above 35. The index generated a median return of 15.5 per cent over the subsequent 12 months, with positive returns in seven of nine observations, or 77.8 per cent. Remarkably, the analysis identified just four completed, non-overlapping signals over the past 25 years when the VXN climbed above 45, highlighting how rare such extreme Nasdaq-100 volatility has been. Following these signals, the Nasdaq-100 generated a median 12-month return of 25.0 per cent, with positive returns in three of four observations. These median returns represent the midpoint of historical outcomes, reducing the influence of unusually large gains or losses. The findings reinforce the potential value of these volatility measures as contrarian indicators: periods of extreme fear have often preceded favourable 12-month equity returns. However, the small number of observations means they should not be viewed as consistently reliable predictors of future performance. Because the Nasdaq-100 typically experiences greater price fluctuations than the S&P 500, VXN readings tend to be higher than those of the VIX. The threshold of 45 therefore provides useful historical perspective on the elevated Nasdaq-100 volatility on Nov.20. When fear is not a buying signal Not every volatility spike precedes a recovery. The dot-com collapse beginning in 2000, market turmoil following the events of Sept. 11, 2001, the global financial crisis of 2008 and the inflation-driven bear market of 2022 illustrate how deeper economic and financial challenges can prolong equity weakness. When volatility coincides with weakening earnings, deteriorating economic conditions or financial instability, markets can remain under pressure. Extreme fear alone does not establish that a market bottom has arrived. Looking beyond market fear Market corrections are not created equal. A decline driven by deteriorating earnings, recessionary conditions or financial instability differs fundamentally from a selloff driven primarily by changing investor sentiment or valuation compression. When share prices fall faster than underlying earnings expectations, valuations become more attractive, potentially improving the outlook for subsequent returns if corporate fundamentals remain resilient. This is particularly relevant for technology and artificial intelligence-related companies, where strong long-term growth prospects can coexist with substantial short-term volatility. Widespread pessimism can create opportunities to acquire fundamentally strong businesses at more attractive valuations. The challenge is distinguishing temporary sentiment shifts from genuine deterioration in business fundamentals. Investor behaviour may be the greatest risk Elevated volatility does not guarantee that markets have bottomed. Even when historical evidence suggests favourable forward returns, further short-term declines remain possible. Maintaining perspective during these periods is essential. Investment decisions should reflect an investor’s long-term objectives, financial goals, risk tolerance, and time horizon, supported by a comprehensive total wealth plan. A disciplined approach can help investors avoid emotional decisions that turn temporary market declines into permanent investment losses. In the end, the greatest investment risk during periods of heightened volatility may not be volatility itself, but investor behaviour.
